claims.text: The Z method can be used with ab initio molecular dynamics to predict melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The Z method can reliably predict melting temperature.
The Z method can predict entropy of fusion.
The Z method can predict enthalpy of fusion.
The Z method can predict volume change at the melting point.
The Z method significantly reduces computational cost relative to full free-energy thermodynamic integration.
In the proposed Z-method simulation, constant-energy dynamics induce spontaneous melting of a superheated solid.
Periodic boundary conditions and constant-energy dynamics allow the system to explore a metastable superheated solid state.
The atomic configurations evolve from an ordered crystal to a disordered liquid during the simulation.
Instability of the superheated solid produces a sudden pressure drop.
Instability of the superheated solid produces a sudden energy drop.
The discontinuity associated with spontaneous melting identifies the melting temperature.
Discontinuities in thermodynamic quantities permit extraction of entropy, enthalpy, and volume changes at melting.
Z-method predictions will agree with available experimental melting benchmarks.
Z-method predictions will agree with prior high-accuracy free-energy integration results.
The method may be less reliable when the simulated system is too small.
The method may be less reliable when transition dynamics are not captured within the simulation time scale.
Accuracy relative to full free-energy methods may depend on material-specific anharmonicity and finite-size effects.
Entropy and enthalpy of fusion can be computed from latent heat release in the proposed simulation.
Volume change at melting can be derived from solid–liquid density differences.

contradictions.description: The simulation is specified as constant-energy dynamics, but the mechanism invokes a sudden energy drop. If 'energy' means conserved total energy, these statements conflict; the hypothesis does not clarify whether the reported drop instead concerns temperature, potential energy, or another energy component.
